definition: Ingenuous means innocently open, frank, and trusting.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ingenuous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ingenuous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: His ingenuous habit of saying exactly what he thought made him a hopeless poker player and a trusted friend.
Frank stops short of ingenuous — a frank speaker is simply direct, with worldly judgment intact.
Gullible goes further than ingenuous — open trust has tipped into being easy prey for any trickster.

Artless means without performance or design — an artless answer is not arranged to impress anyone. Ingenuous keeps that lack of calculation and adds warmth: the ingenuous speaker is not merely unstudied but openly trusting, offering frank confidences in pure good faith.

Trusting means ready to believe what other people say — a disposition toward incoming claims. Ingenuous joins that trust to outgoing openness: frank speech, nothing hidden, no angle. A trusting listener believes easily; an ingenuous speaker also lays her own thoughts bare.
careful about what is revealed, and to whom
watching for tricks, slow to take things at face value
The jeweler confirmed the brooch was a genuine Victorian piece, not a reproduction.
Ingenuous means innocently open, frank, and trusting.

On her first day in the city, the exchange student was entirely ingenuous: she greeted strangers in the elevator, asked a vendor whether his 'world-famous' pretzels were truly famous, and accepted every answer with delighted belief.
Ingenuous means innocently open and trusting—do not confuse it with ingenious, which means brilliantly clever.
An ingenuous question is asked in pure good faith; an ingenious one has a clever design behind it.
Ingenuous praises innocent openness — a child's honesty in an adult conversation.
It is one letter away from ingenious ('brilliantly clever'), and the two mean utterly different things: an ingenuous answer is disarmingly honest, an ingenious one is impressively crafty.
If the sentence is about cleverness, ingenuous is the wrong word.

Her first week at the academy, Palova answered every question anyone asked her, including several nobody had asked.
She told her seatmate which scholarship she was on, told the head of the fencing club she found him intimidating, and told the dean, cheerfully, that his welcome speech had run long.
When an upperclassman sold her a 'reserved seat' in the free library, she thanked him twice.
By October the older students had quietly formed what they called the Palova Patrol, intercepting anyone who looked likely to take advantage of so ingenuous a first-year.
The strange thing, their ringleader admitted, was that nobody wanted her to change.
They only wanted the world to deserve her.
